questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Narrowing a broad topic
questions.learningObjective: narrow a subject label into a question that available evidence could answer
questions.stem: A seminar group is assigned the topic urban water use and must post a workable research question on Friday. Which revision narrows the topic far enough to become answerable with the evidence they can actually gather?

options.text: How does a water-saving notice printed on the bill change reported household use in one district?
What do residents of the district think the water bill should say?
options.misconception: collects stated opinions where the topic calls for a measured outcome

options.text: Whether water is a public good or a private good in law
options.misconception: asks for a classification that no district-level gathering of evidence would settle

options.text: Water use in the modern city as a research topic
options.misconception: keeps the untouched subject label as though it were already a question

questions.explanation: A workable question needs a population, a feature, and an outcome the group could observe in the time it has, and only the first option supplies all three: one district, a notice printed on the bill, and reported household use. The second gathers opinions, which cannot show whether behaviour changed at all. The third asks for a legal classification that no data collected in a district would settle, and the fourth is the assignment restated, still naming a field rather than anything to look at.
questions.hint: Look for the option naming a group, something done to it, and something measurable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Answerability from available evidence
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a question can be answered with the evidence a group can actually reach
questions.stem: Before committing, a group tests four candidate questions against what it can actually reach. Which question survives that test?

options.text: In the county's online rental filings, how often is the same party named as both landlord and mortgage holder?
Do landlords in this county behave responsibly toward the people who rent from them?
options.misconception: asks a broad moral verdict that no set of filing records could deliver

options.text: How do renters feel about the transparency of the county's rental filings?
options.misconception: asks for attitudes that a register of transactions does not contain

options.text: What is the best way for a city to regulate its rental market?
options.misconception: asks for a policy recommendation rather than a finding about records

questions.explanation: Surviving the feasibility test means naming the evidence first and then asking a question that evidence could speak to. The first option names a public register, a population, and a pairing visible inside the register itself. The second asks for a moral verdict that filing data cannot deliver, the third asks how people feel when the source records transactions rather than attitudes, and the fourth asks for a recommendation, which is an outcome of deliberation rather than a finding about records.
questions.hint: Find the option whose named source actually contains the thing being asked about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Questions that presuppose their conclusion
questions.learningObjective: detect a question that assumes the answer it is meant to elicit
questions.stem: A group wants a neutral opener for its reading on a new evening intake session. Which of the four questions is neutral, rather than quietly assuming the outcome it claims to be asking about?

options.text: Does the evening intake session reduce the number of students who miss a first appointment?
Why does the evening intake session turn away students who can only attend in the daytime?
options.misconception: assumes in its why-form that daytime students really are being turned away

options.text: How badly does the evening intake session fail students who hold daytime jobs?
options.misconception: presupposes the failure inside an intensifier rather than leaving the effect open

options.text: Which students are harmed by the evening intake session?
options.misconception: bakes the assumption of harm into the noun so that a negative answer is unavailable

questions.explanation: A neutral opener leaves the effect genuinely open, and only the first option does, since it can be answered yes or no. The why-form in the second option already treats daytime students as being turned away, so the group has chosen its finding before the reading begins. The third builds the same assumption into an intensifier, and the fourth carries it in the noun harm, which removes any answer other than an elaboration.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four could be answered with a flat no without contradicting the question's own wording.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Terms needing a definition first
questions.learningObjective: recognise a question that must have a definition settled before it can be pursued
questions.stem: A group proposes: In what ways does the platform's content moderation contribute to online trust among users aged sixteen to twenty-four? What should the group settle before it starts reading?

options.text: What counts as moderation and what counts as trust, since the members currently use both words in different senses
Which three articles to read first, so the group has a fixed set of texts before it begins
options.misconception: treats a reading order as a substitute for settling the terms the question rests on

options.text: A draft conclusion to aim at, so the group knows what counts as a relevant passage
options.misconception: starts from a conclusion and treats evidence as material selected to fit it

options.text: The platform's own policy document, since it states the goals the moderation is meant to serve
options.misconception: leans on a source that states aims rather than one that defines the group's own terms

questions.explanation: A question whose key words carry more than one sense cannot be researched until the group fixes those senses, because two members can read the same passage and report opposite findings while both are being careful. Only the first option names that problem and pairs each contested word with the definition that must be settled. Fixing a reading order does not stop two readers meaning different things by trust, drafting a conclusion inverts the direction of inquiry, and a policy document reports the organisation's aims without settling what this group will count.
questions.hint: Ask which step prevents two readers from reporting opposite findings on the same sentence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Vocabulary with no cross-field equivalent
questions.learningObjective: explain what is lost when one field's term is carried into another unchanged
questions.stem: A psychologist tells an economics seminar that market equilibrium describes a point at which participants' views stabilise. The economists recognise the term and reject the description. Why?

options.text: The term names a state in which no participant can gain by changing behaviour, which is not what settled opinions describe
The term is technical, and a technical term should not leave the discipline that coined it
options.misconception: makes crossing a discipline boundary the offence rather than a mismatch in meaning

options.text: The economists think settled opinions need describing in their own vocabulary, not in a borrowed one
options.misconception: objects to the borrowed word on stylistic grounds while ignoring what it fails to name

options.text: The term only applies where there is a price, and a seminar discussion has no price in it
options.misconception: fixates on an absent price while missing that the definition itself does not fit

questions.explanation: Carrying a term across fields is defensible only when it still picks out the same thing. Market equilibrium in economics describes a state where no participant can improve their position by changing behaviour, and a group whose opinions have merely stopped moving is a different state, so the transfer loses exactly the content that made the term worth importing. Treating the border itself as the offence misses the point, objecting to the word rather than the mismatch confuses register with reference, and fixing on the missing price ignores that the definition, not the setting, is what fails to match.
questions.hint: Ask what the borrowed term picks out in its home field, then whether this case is that state.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Assumptions carried by a borrowed method
questions.learningObjective: name the assumption a method from another field smuggles into a new setting
questions.stem: A team borrowed a laboratory design to study peer mentoring. They placed thirty mentor pairs in a mentoring group and thirty in a comparison group, withheld mentoring from the comparison group for one semester, scored both groups with the outcome measure the laboratory had used, and reported a larger improvement in the mentored group. Which assumption does the borrowed design carry into this setting?

options.text: That withholding the activity fairly builds a comparison group, which works when the thing withheld does no good but not when it is a relationship participants may need
That thirty pairs per group is a large enough sample, which the team never checked against an expected effect size
options.misconception: fixates on the sample size the passage never justifies instead of how the comparison group was built

options.text: That the laboratory's outcome measure transfers, since the team reused a measure built for a different task
options.misconception: names the borrowed measure, a real weakness, rather than the design assumption the question asks for

options.text: That one semester is long enough for mentoring to show any effect, which the team set to match the term dates
options.misconception: fixates on the length of treatment while ignoring how the comparison group was assembled

questions.explanation: The passage builds its comparison group by removing the very activity under study, and that move is borrowed from experiments on inert substances, where a withheld dose spoils nobody's week. Whether a pair of people can be deprived of mentoring for a semester without loss is a separate question, and the passage never raises it, so the difference the team reports is measured against a group whose experience the design itself created. Sample size, the borrowed measure, and the length of the term are all real features of the passage and all defensible criticisms, but each could be repaired without changing who was in the comparison group.
questions.hint: Look at how the comparison group was assembled rather than at how many people were in it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an analogy stops carrying
questions.learningObjective: locate the point at which a cross-domain analogy stops carrying
questions.stem: A group argues that a city water system is like a household budget, so a leak is like overspending and a reservoir is like a savings account. Which observation most directly shows the analogy breaking down?

options.text: A reservoir holds water for everyone in the system while a savings account belongs to one household, so a release to one user reduces what the rest have
Both a budget and a water system can be itemised, and itemising them makes the comparison easier to follow
options.misconception: treats a shared feature as the flaw when that shared feature is what the analogy runs on

options.text: Overspending can be made good next month, while a shortage of water cannot be made good within a season
options.misconception: picks out a real difference in reversibility that leaves the part-to-part mapping intact

options.text: A budget is written on paper and a water system is built out of pipes, so the two are plainly different
options.misconception: compares the medium of the store rather than the relation the part stands in

questions.explanation: An analogy transfers relations, not merely a look, and the relation it transfers here is who owns and controls a store. A savings account belongs to one household, so drawing on it leaves everyone else untouched, while a reservoir is held in common and a release to one district reduces what is available to the rest, so the part that matched savings was the one whose defining relation does not hold. Itemisation is a feature the analogy actually uses, and a difference in reversibility does not disturb which part stands for which.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the target fails the relation the matching part plays in the source.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant joining claim to reason
questions.learningObjective: identify the unstated bridge between a claim and the reason offered for it
questions.stem: A student argues that students who attend the weekly writing hour submit longer final essays, so the writing hour makes the essays longer. Which sentence states the warrant that has to be accepted for the inference to work?

options.text: Attending the writing hour causes the extra length, rather than the students who already write at length choosing to attend
The longer essays are longer than the essays of students who did not attend the writing hour
options.misconception: restates the reason the argument already supplied instead of bridging it to a cause

options.text: The writing hour should be kept in the timetable, since it produces longer final essays
options.misconception: repeats the conclusion as a recommendation and supplies no bridge at all

options.text: Some students attend the writing hour and some do not, and the two groups differ in several respects
options.misconception: reports the comparison already contained in the premise without adding a cause

questions.explanation: An inference from an observed difference to an effect on that difference needs a bridge saying the difference was produced by the thing under study rather than selected for by it, and the first option is that bridge, stated in the negative because the alternative explanation is what the argument has to exclude. The second repeats the comparison already given as the reason, the third replaces a causal conclusion with a recommendation, and the fourth reports that two groups were compared, which the premise established and which by itself decides nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what must be true about cause and selection for that difference to reach the conclusion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: state the premise an argument depends on without stating
questions.stem: A handout reads: historians of this campaign work almost entirely from surviving officers' letters, and those letters discuss supply more often than any other subject, so the army's real priorities were economic. What must a reader accept, unstated in the passage, before that conclusion follows?

options.text: That what a correspondent chose to write about reflects what the organisation actually wanted, rather than only what the post allowed him to write
That officers wrote candidly rather than shaping their letters to protect themselves from later readers
options.misconception: raises a sincerity worry about the sources instead of the bridge from writing to wanting

options.text: That letters survive in proportion to how important their subject later proved to historians
options.misconception: asks about archive survival while ignoring that survival supplies no bridge to actual priority

options.text: That the word priorities means what one officer wanted rather than what the army as a whole wanted
options.misconception: pursues a dispute over a definition rather than supplying the missing link from text to intent

questions.explanation: The argument moves from what appears in letters to what an organisation wanted, and nothing in the passage licenses that step. Only the first option supplies the missing link, and it is the assumption any reading from documents to intentions makes, one historians argue about rather than accept by default. The other three name real difficulties, since correspondence may be guarded, the archive is a biased sample of what was written, and the passage never fixes the sense of its own key word. But each could be settled while the bridge stayed absent, and the bridge could be defended while all three difficulties stood, so none of them is the premise the conclusion hangs on.
questions.hint: Ask what the passage treats as settled when it moves from letters to institutional intention.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Conclusions that do not follow
questions.learningObjective: explain why a conclusion is unsupported by the premises offered for it
questions.stem: A city replaced every signal on its busiest arterial road last spring, and average travel time along that road has not fallen since. A councillor concludes that the new signal timing was not a factor in the congestion. What makes that inference unsound?

options.text: No improvement along the road is treated as proof of no contribution, when the timing change could have helped while a larger unexamined change pushed travel times the other way
One road cannot show whether a timing plan works, since a plan's effects would be expected to appear across the network
options.misconception: objects to the study site while the passage's own reasoning fails before site selection matters

options.text: An average can conceal the commuters who are now much worse off, so the figure may be hiding the relevant effect
options.misconception: raises a genuine limit of averages while ignoring that the conclusion outruns any figure at all

options.text: No comparison road is offered, so the timing change cannot be separated from everything else that changed
options.misconception: demands a control the passage lacks instead of naming the step from no change to no effect

questions.explanation: The councillor takes a flat outcome and reads it as a null result, but an outcome that has not moved is only a null result once every other possible influence on it has been ruled out, and this passage rules out none. Under the first reading the timing change and some unexamined change pull in opposite directions and the net is zero, which leaves the timing plan very much a factor in the congestion. The other three are separately defensible criticisms, and each could be the strongest objection in a different argument, but all three concern how well the road was measured.
questions.hint: Ask what could be true about the timing change while the average still fails to move.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Objections that add something
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an objection that raises a new consideration from one that repeats the claim
questions.stem: A group proposes replacing the current grading scale, and a classmate replies: So your position is that the current scale is a bad scale. What separates a reply of that kind from a valid concern about the proposal?

options.text: The reply adds nothing the proposal did not already say, whereas a valid concern introduces a consideration the proposal left unanswered
The reply is short, and a short reply usually has less behind it than a longer one would
options.misconception: judges the reply by its length rather than by whether it puts a new consideration on the table

options.text: The reply restates the proposal in the classmate's own words, which is a fair opening move in any discussion
options.misconception: treats restatement as the start of engagement rather than as a way of avoiding it

options.text: The reply is aimed at the scale rather than at the group, so it has picked the wrong target
options.misconception: fixes on the grammatical target while missing that the reply names no new issue at all

questions.explanation: A reply does work in a seminar when it puts something in front of the group that the group can now answer, and a restatement puts nothing there, because the group already knows what it proposed. That is the whole difference between the classmate's sentence and a valid concern, and it is why restatement tends to end a discussion, since there is no question in it for the other side to take up. Length, grammatical target, and being a reasonable opening move are all worth something, but a short reply can carry a decisive consideration and a restatement in three sentences can carry nothing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the group could answer the reply with something it had not already been asked.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Adjudicating two incompatible readings
questions.learningObjective: choose a way to settle a clash between two readings of one passage
questions.stem: Two students read the same short essay. One concludes that its restraint is a deliberate rhetorical strategy. The other concludes that it is simply the author's temperament. How should the seminar adjudicate the clash rather than simply vote on it?

options.text: Ask each reader which features of the text would count as evidence for that reading, then check whether the text supplies those features
Take the reading more members of the seminar find convincing, since a shared seminar is a shared audience
options.misconception: settles a question about the text by counting preferences in one particular room

options.text: Accept both readings, since interpretive disagreement shows the essay supports more than one meaning
options.misconception: declares the pair equally valid, which answers a different question from the one asked

options.text: Defer to the reader who prepared most thoroughly, since preparation is the seminar's first stated requirement
options.misconception: hands the question to effort alone, which is unrelated to what the text supports

questions.explanation: When two readings of one text cannot both be right, the useful question is what each commits the text to and whether the text meets that commitment, and the first option is the only move that produces an answer the group can check. A count of preferences records the room's mood at a moment rather than anything in the text, and treating both readings as settled is a decision about what to do with interpretive plurality, not an adjudication of the clash, so it leaves the disagreement exactly where it was.
questions.hint: Ask what each reading would have to find in the text, then go looking for it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Weight carried by primary and secondary sources
questions.learningObjective: assign different evidential weight to an original record and a later account of it
questions.stem: A group cites a historian's book published in 2018, and the book quotes a letter written in 1911. Which statement assigns the two sources their proper weight?

options.text: The book supports claims about the 2018 historian's reading, while a claim about the letter rests on that historian's selection and transcription until the letter itself is read
The letter supports a claim about what its author wrote, and the book only confirms that the letter is authentic
options.misconception: reduces the secondary source to an authenticity stamp instead of an interpretation with its own errors

options.text: The book is the better evidence because a historian has checked the letter against others, and the letter is only a draft
options.misconception: treats later interpretation as verification of the earlier text and demotes the record itself

options.text: Both support the same claim equally, since one source is old and the other new, and age and recency divide neatly
options.misconception: weighs the sources by age against recency instead of by the job each was made to do

questions.explanation: The two sources were made to do different jobs, and the weight follows the job. A letter is evidence about what one person wrote on one occasion, and it says nothing by itself about what that person believed or what an institution wanted. A book written in 2018 is evidence about how a historian selected, transcribed, and framed that letter, so a group's claim about the letter inherits everything the historian chose to include and to leave out.
questions.hint: Ask what each source was produced to do, then match the claim to that job.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Summaries that preserve structure
questions.learningObjective: choose the summary that keeps an argument's shape rather than its content list
questions.stem: An argument runs: the fund raised its fees twice, fees are the main cost small savers face, and small savers therefore stopped saving. Which summary preserves the structure of that argument?

options.text: It argues from a rise in the fund's fees, through their effect on small savers' main cost, to the consequence that those savers stopped saving
The fund raised its fees twice, small savers were affected, and the discussion closes with a claim about saving behaviour
options.misconception: lists the three contents in order but drops the chain of dependence running between them

options.text: The argument says the fund is badly run and that small savers ought to be protected from fees of this kind
options.misconception: replaces the argument with an evaluation the original never reaches

options.text: Two fee increases are mentioned, and the second of them is the one the argument depends on
options.misconception: invents a ranking the argument does not make and drops the reasoning entirely

questions.explanation: A structural summary keeps the three slots and the dependence running between them, because the argument's force lives in the word therefore, and only the first option preserves a rise, a cost, and a consequence joined in that order. The second lists the same three contents and loses the links, which is the failure a summary usually has, since a reader coming away with the topics has none of the reasoning. The third supplies a verdict the argument never reaches, and the fourth invents a ranking while leaving out the step from cost to behaviour.
questions.hint: Check whether a reader could reconstruct the word therefore after reading the summary.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest
questions.learningObjective: restate a view you accept in a form that could actually be answered
questions.stem: A group member says the current reading list is fine and that anyone who complains simply does not like hard books. A classmate asks for the strongest version of the complaint before replying. What does that request repair?

options.text: It replaces a claim about the complainers' motives, which nothing in the reading list could settle, with a claim about the list that could be settled
It makes the complaint harder to dismiss, so the reply has to be a stronger argument rather than a sharper insult
options.misconception: frames the move as a debating tactic aimed at the reply instead of a repair of the claim

options.text: It slows the exchange down, which gives the group time to gather the evidence it does not yet have in hand
options.misconception: credits the request with buying time rather than with changing what is being claimed

options.text: It shows respect for the classmate, which is the seminar's first norm and the reason for asking at all
options.misconception: reads a methodological repair as a social courtesy that has no argumentative effect

questions.explanation: The sentence as spoken makes two moves, and the second is fatal to the exchange, because a claim about who dislikes hard books cannot be settled with anything anyone can read, while a claim about what the list does to a reader's workload can. Framing it as a tactic, as time-buying, or as politeness describes things a question can also be, but none explains why this one makes the argument answerable.

options.misconception: quietly lowers the proposal to a milder one and answers a position nobody actually held

options.misconception: declines to reconstruct anything at all by treating the matter as already decided

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sympathetic reading of a weak argument
questions.learningObjective: read a weak argument charitably without pretending its gap is not there
questions.stem: A handout argues that the seminar should stop assigning readings, because students who are not reading them are only pretending to read anyway. What does a sympathetic reading do with the weakest point in that argument?

options.text: Treat the claim that pretended reading is a waste as the argument's real concern, while still recording that pretending has not been shown to occur
Conclude that the argument is simply wrong, since no one could ever support a claim about what other students are pretending
options.misconception: dismisses the argument outright instead of separating its concern from its unsupported claim

options.text: Assume the writer meant that assigned reading is generally wasted, and read the argument as making that point instead
options.misconception: silently substitutes a different claim so that the original can be rescued from its gap

options.text: Accept the argument as it stands, since reading a view sympathetically means taking it at face value
options.misconception: confuses charity with agreement, which removes the standard the reading is supposed to apply

questions.explanation: Charity is a division of labour, asking what the argument would be like if its reasoning were sound while leaving that reasoning exactly as it is. Under the first reading the writer's concern is a real waste, one that a seminar full of quiet preparers would recognise, and the gap the argument leaves is the unsupported step from not reading to pretending. The second treats a weak premise as a reason for dismissing a concern that may be legitimate, the third rescues the argument by rewriting it into a claim the writer never made, and the fourth mistakes reading a view sympathetically for agreeing with it.
questions.hint: Ask what the argument would look like if its gap were filled in, without filling it in.

questions.topic: Narrowing a topic in two steps

options.text: Evidence and citation, since a question is only ever as good as the sources behind it

options.misconception: asks about a period the group cannot reach through the records it has any access to

options.text: Why do archivists disagree about how they describe material that has no obvious date?
options.misconception: asks for the causes of a professional disagreement the group has no way to sample

options.text: Should the university archive follow national cataloguing standards in every particular respect?
options.misconception: asks for a policy judgement rather than a finding that any record could support

questions.explanation: A question has to name something the group can reach, something it can count, and something that could come out either way, and the first option does all three, since the archive's own catalogue holds dated entries, the number of disagreements is countable, and a rate of disagreement is not settled in advance. The second reaches a century the group cannot examine through its access, the third asks about the causes of a professional disagreement without any way of sampling archivists, and the fourth asks for a recommendation, which is what a seminar concludes rather than what it researches.
questions.hint: Ask which question names a countable thing the group can actually open.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Answerability before advocacy
questions.learningObjective: explain why a group should make its claim answerable before defending it
questions.stem: Explain why a group should get its claim into a form that could be answered before it begins arguing for that claim.

answer.exemplar: A claim can only be defended if something could have come out the other way, so answerability is a precondition of argument rather than a courtesy extended to the other side. If a group says its seminar is better because discussion feels more open, nothing could count against that, so every reply it receives is a matter of taste rather than of evidence and the exchange has no result to report. Writing the claim in an answerable form costs the group something real, because it gives the other side a precise target and it may lose. It buys two things in return. The group learns which of its reasons is actually load-bearing, since an attack on a precise claim lands on a particular premise and leaves the rest standing, and it also learns whether its claim was ever supported, which it cannot discover while the question is closed to evidence. In a seminar where preparation is measured by what a member can do with a challenge, a claim that cannot be challenged is not a strong position but an unexamined one.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that an unanswerable claim converts every reply into a matter of taste, names the real cost of answerability, which is that a precise claim gives the other side a target, and names the two things bought in return, a way of finding which premise is load-bearing and a way of discovering whether the claim was ever supported.
questions.hint: Ask what a group cannot learn about its own claim while nobody could answer it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Reconstructing a rejected view as a duty
questions.learningObjective: justify reconstructing an opposing view at its strongest
questions.stem: Explain why a group owes an opposing view a reconstruction at its strongest, rather than replying to the weakest version of it that happens to be available.

answer.exemplar: Rebuilding a view at its strongest is a requirement of good argument, not a courtesy extended to people whose conclusions the group dislikes. A weak version is easy to defeat and defeats nothing, so a group that answers one has shown only that it can knock down a position nobody was actually defending, while its own claim goes unexamined. The people who hold the view have not been given the chance to bring their real reasons, so the group learns nothing about whether its own position would survive contact with the best case against it. The second reason is less comfortable, because the discipline exposes the group to the one objection that matters. To state an opposing case so well that its adherents would accept the statement is to discover whether it might be better than the position the group is defending, and a group that cannot state that case has no way of knowing whether it disagrees with the view or only with the version of it it happened to hear in the room.

questions.explanation: A strong response says that defeating a weak version proves nothing about the strong one, that the people holding the view are then never asked for their real reasons, and turns the discipline on the group itself, since the case a group cannot state is one it has not really tested its own position against.
questions.hint: Ask what a group learns about its own claim after it has answered the weakest version available.
